doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: The through line: playing, his uncle's warning, and featuring other soloists
summary: He loves making music, kept playing despite his uncle's warning, and features better saxophonists in his big bands.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Last question. Of all the things you’ve done from going into clubs and sitting in to standing in front of a 60-piece orchestra, is there a through line through that? Is there something that is always a constant for you?

Gee. I mean I’m just totally enamored of making music in some way. So to stand in front of my quartet and play, “I Wish I Knew” or an obscure standard is just as exciting as doing a downbeat in front of the London Symphony Orchestra. It’s a different excitement I guess. But it’s still an extension of exactly where I was when I started, which not a lot of people can say that. The one thing that — when I saw my uncle a lot when he moved to America and I was in America, and he was basically conducting for Milton Berle and Anthony Newley and Donald O’Connor and, you know, doing a lot of variety stuff. And he said to me — he was a great trombone player, recorded with Coleman Hawkins in the ‘30s and he said, “Have you given up playing yet?” And I said, “No.” He said, “You will.” I said, “No, I won’t.” So it made me more determined to keep the playing going. Because he’d put his trombone behind the chair and forgotten about it. And that’s I guess a lot of arrangers’ lot isn’t it, that they stop playing because they just don’t have time to devote to it. I mean I stopped playing flute and clarinet possibly for that reason, but I never wanted to stop playing saxophone or playing in public or you know having a jazz group or using the jazz brain.
I’d like to think that that’s important, that you’re still connected in a physical way to the players who are making your music come alive, and you still know what that feels like.

Oh I’m always conscious of it, particularly, you know the interesting thing, somebody said, “Why don’t you feature yourself more with your big band?” And I said, “Because there are five saxophone players who are better than me and I want to hear them.” You know I don’t mind playing three numbers in the whole show, you know that’s fine as long as I can hear some of these brilliant players. And I had a big band in L.A. and a big band in Australia and one is the U.K. and they’re all fantastic. You know when you’ve got Pete Christlieb or Plas Johnson or Bob Efford sitting there, you’re not going to hog every solo. There’s no way. Or Lanny Morgan. You know it’s insanity to think — well you know what, I’m going to feature myself now, never mind those people.
